title: Learn the Essential Built-In Commands
tip: Claude Code has several built-in slash commands that control session behavior. Knowing the core set covers 90% of your day-to-day needs. Type /help at any time for a full list.
example:
# Core built-in commands:
/help          # Show all available commands
/clear         # Clear conversation history (fresh start)
/compact       # Summarize conversation to free context window
/config        # View and edit configuration settings
/status        # Show current session status and context usage
/cost          # Show token usage and cost for this session
/exit          # End the session

# Usage:
/compact       # When you see context warnings
/clear         # When starting a completely new unrelated task
why: Built-in commands give you direct control over session state. /compact and /clear are especially important for long working sessions where context management matters.

title: Use /help to Discover Available Commands
tip: /help shows all available commands including both built-in Claude Code commands and any custom commands you've defined in .claude/commands/. Run it whenever you're unsure what's available.
example:
# In Claude Code session:
/help

# Output shows:
# Built-in commands:
#   /clear, /compact, /config, /cost, /exit, /help, /status...
#
# Project commands (from .claude/commands/):
#   /review, /test, /deploy, /changelog...
#
# Each command shows its description so you know when to use it
why: /help is your first stop for discoverability. It shows exactly what's available in your current project without reading documentation or files.

title: Use /compact Strategically to Extend Sessions
tip: /compact summarizes conversation history to free up context space, allowing you to continue a long session. Use it proactively before hitting limits, not reactively when you've already lost context.
example:
# Watch for context usage indicators, then:
/compact

# After compacting, orient Claude to continue:
'We were working on the payment module. The next step is
implementing the webhook verification. The relevant files
are src/webhooks/stripe.ts and src/services/PaymentService.ts.'

# Pro tip: compact at logical boundaries, not mid-task:
# Bad: /compact in the middle of implementing a function
# Good: /compact after completing a feature, before starting the next
why: Proactive compacting preserves important context in the summary. Reactive compacting after hitting the limit means Claude may have already lost critical context.

title: Use /clear When Starting Unrelated Tasks
tip: /clear wipes the conversation history completely, starting fresh. Use it when switching to a completely different task where the existing context would be irrelevant or confusing.
example:
# Scenario: You just finished debugging the auth system.
# Now you want to work on a completely unrelated UI component.

/clear

# Then start fresh:
'I need to build a DateRangePicker component. Requirements:
- Two date inputs (start and end)
- Calendar popup on focus
- Highlight date range between selections...
[etc]'

# The auth debugging context is gone — Claude starts fresh
# without the mental overhead of irrelevant auth discussions
why: Leftover context from previous tasks can subtly influence Claude's responses. /clear ensures each new task gets focused attention without contamination from unrelated work.

title: Configure Claude Code Behavior with /config
tip: /config opens the Claude Code configuration editor where you can set your model, API key, editor preferences, and other session defaults. Changes persist to your local config file.
example:
# Open config:
/config

# Key settings you'll configure:
# model: claude-opus-4-5 (or sonnet, haiku based on your needs)
# apiKey: your Anthropic API key
# editor: vscode (or your preferred editor)
# theme: dark/light
# verbosity: normal/verbose/quiet

# Or set specific values directly:
/config set model claude-sonnet-4-5
/config set theme dark
why: /config lets you tune Claude Code for your workflow without editing config files manually. Especially useful for switching models when you need speed vs. capability.

title: Create Custom Commands with Markdown Files
tip: Custom commands are markdown files in .claude/commands/. The filename becomes the command name (e.g., review.md becomes /review). The file content is the prompt template sent to Claude.
example:
# Create .claude/commands/review.md:
Review the code changes in the current working directory.

Perform a comprehensive review covering:
1. Correctness: logic errors, edge cases, off-by-one errors
2. Security: injection risks, auth checks, input validation
3. Performance: unnecessary loops, N+1 queries, blocking calls
4. Code quality: naming, readability, single responsibility
5. Tests: coverage gaps, missing edge case tests

Format output as: Issue | File:Line | Severity | Suggestion

# Use it:
/review
why: Custom commands encode your team's recurring workflows as reusable prompts. Anyone on the team can run /review and get consistent, thorough output without remembering the full prompt.

title: Add Frontmatter to Custom Commands for Metadata
tip: Add YAML frontmatter to custom command files to provide a description and configure behavior. The description appears in /help output, making commands discoverable.
example:
# .claude/commands/changelog.md
---
description: Generate a CHANGELOG.md entry from recent git commits
allowed-tools:
  - Bash
  - Write
---

Generate a CHANGELOG.md entry for the changes since the last git tag.

1. Run `git log $(git describe --tags --abbrev=0)..HEAD --oneline` to get recent commits
2. Categorize commits by type (feat/fix/docs/etc)
3. Format as Keep a Changelog format (## [Unreleased])
4. Append to the top of CHANGELOG.md
5. Show me the new entry before writing
why: Frontmatter descriptions appear in /help, making your command library self-documenting. allowed-tools restricts which tools the command can use, improving safety.

title: Use the $ARGUMENTS Variable for Parameterized Commands
tip: The $ARGUMENTS variable in custom commands captures everything typed after the command name, allowing you to create parameterized commands that work on specific files, modules, or inputs.
example:
# .claude/commands/test.md
---
description: Write comprehensive tests for a specific file
---
Write comprehensive unit tests for the file at: $ARGUMENTS

1. Read the file to understand its exports and interfaces
2. Create a test file at the corresponding __tests__ path
3. Cover all exported functions with happy path + edge cases
4. Run the tests and fix any failures
5. Report: N tests written, all passing

# Usage:
/test src/services/PaymentService.ts
/test src/utils/date-helpers.ts
why: $ARGUMENTS makes commands reusable across different targets. Without it, you'd need a separate command file for each module you want to test, document, or analyze.

title: Organize Commands in Subdirectories with Namespacing
tip: Group related commands in subdirectories under .claude/commands/. Claude Code namespaces them with a colon (e.g., db/migrate.md becomes /db:migrate). This keeps your command library organized as it grows.
example:
# Organized command structure:
.claude/commands/
  db/
    db-migrate.md      # /db:migrate
    db-seed.md         # /db:seed
    db-reset.md        # /db:reset
  tests/
    test-unit.md       # /tests:unit
    test-integration.md # /tests:integration
    test-coverage.md   # /tests:coverage
  deploy/
    deploy-staging.md  # /deploy:staging
    deploy-prod.md     # /deploy:prod

# Usage:
/db:migrate
/tests:coverage
why: Namespacing prevents collisions and makes large command libraries navigable. Tab completion shows /db: commands grouped together, making discovery intuitive.

title: Create Project-Specific Commands for Recurring Workflows
tip: Identify tasks you do repeatedly in a project (code review, generating boilerplate, running diagnostics) and encode them as project-specific commands. Commit them to the repo so the whole team benefits.
example:
# .claude/commands/new-route.md
---
description: Scaffold a new Express API route with tests and docs
---
Create a new API route for: $ARGUMENTS

Follow the existing pattern from src/routes/users.ts:
1. Create src/routes/$ARGUMENTS.ts with CRUD operations
2. Create src/routes/__tests__/$ARGUMENTS.test.ts
3. Register the route in src/app.ts (after the last existing route)
4. Add JSDoc with OpenAPI annotations for each endpoint
5. Run tests and fix any failures

# Use it:
/new-route products
/new-route orders
/new-route webhooks
why: Project-specific commands capture tribal knowledge about how your project works. A new team member can run /new-route and get a correctly-wired route without studying the codebase.

title: Share Commands via the Repository for Team Consistency
tip: Commit your .claude/commands/ directory to version control. This ensures all team members have the same commands available and the command library evolves with the project.
example:
# .gitignore — DO commit commands, DON'T commit personal settings:
# .claude/settings.local.json  # personal settings (gitignore this)
# .claude/commands/            # commit this — shared team commands
# .claude/agents/              # commit this — shared team agents

# Commit the command library:
git add .claude/commands/
git commit -m 'chore: add claude code team command library'

# Add to your onboarding docs:
# 'Run /help to see available Claude Code commands for this project'
why: Commands in version control are a living library of team knowledge. They improve over time as the team adds commands, and new team members get the full library immediately on clone.

title: Build Multi-Step Workflow Commands
tip: Commands can encode complex multi-step workflows that orchestrate reading, analysis, file creation, and validation. Think of them as macros for entire development workflows.
example:
# .claude/commands/feature-complete.md
---
description: Mark a feature complete: tests, docs, PR description, and changelog
allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob]
---
Mark the feature in $ARGUMENTS as complete.

## Completion Checklist

### 1. Test Coverage
- Run `npm test -- --coverage --collectCoverageFrom=$ARGUMENTS`
- If coverage < 80%, write missing tests

### 2. Documentation
- Read $ARGUMENTS and check all public functions have JSDoc
- Add missing JSDoc comments

### 3. Lint
- Run `npx eslint $ARGUMENTS --fix`

### 4. PR Description
- Generate a PR description and save to .claude/pr-description.md

### 5. Changelog
- Add entry to CHANGELOG.md under [Unreleased]

Report completion status of each step.
why: Multi-step workflow commands eliminate the repetitive overhead of feature completion tasks. Run one command and get tests, docs, lint, and PR prep done automatically.

title: Chain Commands with Context Passing
tip: Design commands that pass context to subsequent commands via shared files. Command A writes context to .claude/tmp/, Command B reads it. This enables command chaining without putting everything in one giant command.
example:
# Command 1: /analyze saves analysis to a temp file
# .claude/commands/analyze.md
Analyze the codebase for architecture issues.
Save findings as JSON to .claude/tmp/analysis.json:
{
  "issues": [...],
  "priority_files": [...],
  "suggested_refactors": [...]
}

# Command 2: /fix-top reads from that file
# .claude/commands/fix-top.md
Read .claude/tmp/analysis.json (from previous /analyze run).
Fix the top 3 highest-priority issues found.
For each fix: read the file, apply the fix, run tests.

# Workflow:
/analyze       # Builds the analysis
/fix-top       # Fixes top issues from that analysis
why: Context passing via files creates composable command pipelines. Each command is focused and independently testable, but they chain together for powerful workflows.

title: Create Commands That Invoke Agents
tip: Commands can invoke agents for parts of their workflow, combining the simplicity of a command interface with the specialization of agents. Use this for tasks that need multiple specialist perspectives.
example:
# .claude/commands/full-review.md
---
description: Comprehensive review using specialist agents
allowed-tools: [Read, Bash, Agent]
---
Perform a comprehensive review of $ARGUMENTS using specialist agents.

## Review Pipeline

1. Invoke the security-auditor agent on $ARGUMENTS
   - Collect findings to security-findings.json

2. Invoke the performance-analyzer agent on $ARGUMENTS
   - Collect findings to perf-findings.json

3. Invoke the test-coverage-checker agent on $ARGUMENTS
   - Collect findings to test-findings.json

4. Synthesize all three reports into a final review:
   - Prioritize issues by severity
   - Group related issues
   - Create an action plan

# Usage:
/full-review src/services/PaymentService.ts
why: Commands that invoke agents get the best of both worlds: the simple /command interface for humans, and specialist agent depth for the actual analysis.

title: Build Template Commands with Variable Substitution
tip: Create template commands that use $ARGUMENTS to generate boilerplate for new modules, features, or components following your project's exact structure and patterns.
example:
# .claude/commands/new-service.md
---
description: Scaffold a new service with all required files and patterns
---
Create a new service called '$ARGUMENTS' following our service architecture.

## Files to Create
1. src/services/$ARGUMENTS.ts — service class
2. src/services/__tests__/$ARGUMENTS.test.ts — tests
3. src/services/types/$ARGUMENTS.types.ts — TypeScript types
4. src/services/index.ts — add export (don't create, update existing)

## Pattern to Follow
Copy the structure from src/services/UserService.ts.
Replace 'User' with '$ARGUMENTS' (preserving capitalization).
Update the model reference to use the $ARGUMENTS model if it exists.

## After Creation
Run `npm test -- $ARGUMENTS` and fix any template errors.

# Usage:
/new-service Order
/new-service Notification
why: Template commands standardize new file creation across the team. Everyone gets the same structure, same test setup, and same type organization without copying and renaming manually.

title: Create Diagnostic Commands for Project Health
tip: Build commands that run a suite of health checks on your project and produce a structured status report. Use these for CI integration or regular project health monitoring.
example:
# .claude/commands/health-check.md
---
description: Run comprehensive project health checks and generate report
allowed-tools: [Read, Bash, Glob, Grep]
---
Run a complete project health check and produce a structured report.

## Checks to Run
1. `npm run typecheck` — TypeScript errors
2. `npm run lint` — Lint issues
3. `npm test -- --passWithNoTests` — Test failures
4. `npm audit --audit-level=high` — Security vulnerabilities
5. Count TODO/FIXME comments: `grep -r 'TODO\|FIXME' src/ | wc -l`
6. Check for console.log statements: `grep -r 'console.log' src/ | wc -l`
7. Count test files vs source files ratio

## Output Format
Produce a health score (0-100) and markdown report saved to .claude/health-report.md
why: Diagnostic commands provide instant project health visibility. Running /health-check before a release or sprint review surfaces issues that might otherwise slip through.

title: Use Plugin-Style Commands for Team Knowledge Base
tip: Structure your command library as a team knowledge base, where each command encodes expert knowledge about your domain. Commands should capture the 'how to do X correctly in this project' for common tasks.
example:
# Commands as encoded expertise:

# .claude/commands/safe-deploy.md — encodes deployment runbook
Deploy to staging using our safe deploy procedure:
1. Run `npm run validate` — fail if any checks fail
2. Create a deploy tag: `git tag deploy/$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M)`
3. Run `npm run build` and verify build succeeds
4. Check .env.staging has all required keys (see .env.example)
5. Run `npm run migrate:staging` for pending migrations
6. Deploy with `./scripts/deploy.sh staging`
7. Run smoke tests: `npm run test:smoke -- --env=staging`
8. If any step fails: rollback with `./scripts/rollback.sh staging`

# This encodes your entire deployment runbook as a command
why: Commands that encode procedures are living runbooks that never go stale (they live with the code), are always available, and execute correctly rather than being misremembered.

title: Version and Namespace Commands for Large Teams
tip: For large teams with many commands, add version numbers and owner namespaces to prevent collision and enable gradual migration when commands change significantly.
example:
# Versioned commands for major workflow changes:
.claude/commands/
  review/
    review-v1.md    # /review:v1 — original review prompt
    review-v2.md    # /review:v2 — new review with security focus
    review.md       # /review — current stable version (copy of v2)
  deploy/
    deploy-legacy.md  # /deploy:legacy — old deploy workflow
    deploy.md         # /deploy — current workflow

# Transition strategy:
# 1. Create v2 alongside v1
# 2. Test v2 with the team
# 3. Once stable, update the unversioned command
# 4. Keep v1 available during transition
# 5. Remove v1 after everyone has migrated
why: Versioning commands allows gradual migration. Teams don't have to update all their workflows immediately when a command improves — they can transition at their own pace.
